en: The *Tattvayāthārthyadīpana*, composed by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, son of Śrī Bhāvāviśvanātha Dīkṣita;
composed by Śrī Bhāvāgaṇeśa.
Salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra.
Victorious is that primordial Puruṣa and she, the sovereign Prakṛti, by whom, having conjoined, infinite millions of Brahmāṇḍas are created. // 1 //
I bow to the teachers Kapila, Asuri, and Pañcaśikha, and to the most excellent masters of realized knowledge, for the increase of my intellect and for the accomplishment of all undertakings. (2)
Relying upon the aphorisms of the compendium and the commentary of Pañcaśikha,
Bhāvāgaṇeśa composes this *Tattvayāthārthyadīpana*.

In this regard, first, the knowledge of the person as distinct [from the gunas] is the means to liberation. By means of three aphorisms, he indicates both that from which the person must be distinguished and that which is to be distinguished:
[Aphorism 1: "The eight primal natures."
They are called *prakṛtis* because they act with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*).
The general definition of being a *prakṛti* is the state of initiating another reality (*tattvāntara*).
These [eight] consist of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
In this context, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is eternal, devoid of qualities such as sound, and consists of the three qualities (*guṇa*)—sattva and the rest.
One definition is that the qualities characterized by a state of equilibrium constitute *prakṛti*;
another is that the qualities are not effects (*akārya*).

Likewise, synonyms for *prakṛti* include the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), Brahman, the Imperishable (*akṣara*), the Field (*kṣetra*), Darkness (*tamas*), Māyā, the Vedic Knowledge (*brāhmī vidyā*), Nescience (*avidyā*), Nature (*prakṛti*), Power (*śakti*), the Unborn (*ajā*), and so forth.
It should not be suspected that *prakṛti* is something distinct from the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* while simultaneously possessing those qualities;
rather, the qualities themselves are *prakṛti*.

The Sāṃkhya-pravacana-sūtra states that "sattva and the others do not have those [qualities] as their nature because they are of that form," thereby negating that sattva and the others are attributes of *prakṛti* on the grounds that they constitute the very essence of *prakṛti*.
Consequently, statements such as "the quality (*guṇa*) of *prakṛti*" should be understood as being like the expression "the trees of the forest.

Furthermore, the statement that "sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities born of *prakṛti*"—which asserts they are effects of *prakṛti*—must refer specifically to the *sattva* and other qualities that serve as the causes of the principle of *mahat*, since it would otherwise contradict the scriptural declarations regarding the eternity of the *guṇas*.

For the creation of the Great Principle (mahat) and the others is heard [in scripture] to arise from the inequality of the qualities (guṇa-vaiṣamya); and that inequality is a transformation of the causal qualities (kāraṇa-guṇa-pariṇāma) which, through the combination of homogeneous elements, becomes fit for the conventional usage of "sattva" and so forth, being endowed with results such as illumination.
By this, the position of twenty-eight principles (tattva) should also be understood as established.
I maintain that although the triad beginning with *sattva* possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), they are called "qualities" (*guṇa*) because they serve as instruments for the person (*puruṣa*).
Their substantiality is established by their possession of conjunction, disjunction, and so forth, and by their being material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
As for the common report that these consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, this is due to the non-difference between the property and the substratum (*dharma-dharmin-abheda*).
This is because the mind consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Furthermore, according to the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra*, "Each of those [qualities], such as *sattva* and the rest, possesses its own number and individuality; there is both similarity and dissimilarity among the qualities through properties such as lightness.

For in this sūtra, it is stated that many instances of *sattva* share similarity by virtue of lightness and so forth, while they possess dissimilarity from *rajas* and *tamas* by virtue of those same properties.
Thus, having stated the similarities and differences between many *rajas* (passion) and many *tamas* (darkness) through qualities such as lightness and heaviness respectively,
the mention of their "triple nature" (*tritva*) is based solely on the three classifying attributes (*vibhājakopādhi*) of *sattva*-ness and so forth— just as the Vaiśeṣikas speak of nine substances.
And these [qualities], *sattva* and the others, possess atomic or all-pervading dimensions according to their respective functions.
If [the self] were of intermediate size, it would follow that it is impermanent;
if all [selves] were omnipresent, the localized nature of effects would be untenable,
as it is only logical for the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) of space to be omnipresent.

If it is argued that this contradicts the Sāṃkhya tenet that primordial nature (prakṛti) is unlimited, unitary, and inactive, it is not so; for primordial nature is all-pervasive, just as fragrance pervades the earth. And that all-pervasiveness consists in its being a non-limiting factor for the counter-correlativity of spatial absence (daiśikābhāvapratiyogitānavacchedakatva).
Unity means the absence of plurality due to the diversity of creation;
and inactivity means the absence of specific actions such as determination, self-conceit, and so forth;
otherwise, the agitation of primordial nature (prakṛti) established by the Śruti and Smṛti would be untenable.

The inference regarding primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is as follows: the subject (*pakṣa*) is the effect consisting of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth; the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "it is the effect of a substance whose essence consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion"; the logical reason (*hetu*) is "because, while being an effect, it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion"; and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like beds, seats, and other effects such as clothing.
Here, scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*) serve as the corroborating reasoning (*tarka*).

If it is objected: "Since pleasure is experienced only internally, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the pleasure inherent in beds, seats, and so forth, by which they could serve as examples?"—we reply: No, because according to the principle that "the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect," pleasure, pain, and delusion are established in objects, which are effects composed of the three *guṇas*.

This is evident not only from the cognition "the form of a jar" but also from cognitions of pleasure such as "the pleasure of sandalwood" and "the pleasure of a woman," [which occur] with respect to the object.

Because pleasure and so forth are appropriate [to the object], and because they produce pleasure and pain, pleasure, pain, and the like are established as residing in that very [object]. Furthermore, pleasure and so forth are established in the object by virtue of being the cause of pleasure and so forth in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Moreover, because a single individual entity, such as a woman, produces pleasure and pain through different factors such as time, pleasure, pain, and the like are established as residing in that very [entity].
Thus concludes the exposition of the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti).
Now, intellect (*buddhi*) is defined.
The first definition is: intellect is the primordial effect consisting of the three *guṇas*.
The second definition is: intellect is the internal organ whose function is ascertainment (*niścaya*).
Because it is endowed with excellent qualities known as knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty, it receives the designation "the Great" (mahat); this too is the third characteristic.
Its synonyms are:

mind (manas), intellect (mati), the Great (mahān), Brahmā, primordial consciousness (pūrva-buddhi), function (vṛtti), manifestation (khyāti), wisdom (prajñā), continuity (santati), and memory (smṛti).
And in the Anusmṛti:
"The Great Self, Mati, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, and the heroic Śambhu; likewise Buddhi, Prajñā, Upalabdhi, Brahmā, Vṛtti, and Smṛti."
By these synonymous terms, the Great Self is described:
having hands and feet everywhere, and having eyes, heads, and faces on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading all;
and so do those who possess knowledge, who are free from greed, and who have conquered their anger.
"All these, when liberated, indeed attain greatness;
moreover, in the primary creations, Viṣṇu himself becomes the Lord Svayambhū.

This very principle of Mahat, having undergone transformation through a partial admixture of *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīvas*); joined with demerit and other qualities, it also becomes limited.
"Mahat is the opposite of the Great Obscuration (mahad-uparāga)," according to the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra*.
Of the tree of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the triad of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and Manas, the principle of Mahat (*mahattattva*) is the state of the sprout.
In this regard, regarding the sequence of creation beginning with "From Prakṛti comes Mahat," scripture alone is the authority.

This very principle of Mahat is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the self-existent Lord of effects; by means of that very adjunct, He is omniscient, the Lord of all, the creator of all, the protector of all, and the destroyer of all. As stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*:
"From Pradhāna, together with its modifications, the principle of Mahat was born."
It is called "Great" because the renown [of it] always arises among the worlds.
"From the qualities (guṇas) being agitated, three gods were born;
one single form, the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
And that Self-born One (svayambhū), possessing the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and having the principle of Mahat alone as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), is called Sūtrātman.

That same [state] is called *prājña* because of its partial dissolution (*ardhalaya*) during half-sleep; however, in full sleep, because one abides in the nature of non-distinct pure consciousness through total dissolution, it is called *īśvara* in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. Thus it is said in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa]: "The Great One (*mahat*) is threefold: Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa."
It has been stated in the verse that at the beginning, Viṣṇu alone manifests himself even for the sake of Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
Among the previously mentioned categories such as dharma and so forth, by "dharma" upward movement is meant; by upward movement, the places of enjoyment are indicated.
By this, the subterranean realms (pātāla), the earth, heaven, and so on, are also included.
Liberation comes through knowledge, while dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) results from dispassion for one who is ignorant of the principle of the Puruṣa.
Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa concerning those who contemplate primordial nature: "Those free from the fever [of worldly existence] remain for a full hundred thousand [years]."

Here, by the mention of "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*), the intellect (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the elements, and the sense organs are also included. In that regard, it is heard in scripture immediately following the preceding statement that dissolution into primordial nature occurs when those various [principles] are meditated upon as the Self, preceded by dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten manvantaras;
those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred, while those who contemplate the ego remain for a thousand.
And it is said: "Ten thousand Buddhās remain free from the fever [of suffering].

This is called the natural (prākṛtika) bondage by the yogis; the bondage consisting of the states of the great principle (mahat) and so forth is called the modified (vaikṛtika) bondage. Sovereignty (aiśvarya) is the absence of obstruction, and sovereignty consists of the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Thus, intelligence has been explained.
The ego (ahaṅkāra) is now explained.
From the principle of the Great One (mahattattva), the ego arises, like a branch from a sprout.
And because it possesses a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of "I," it is designated by the name "ego."
The first definition is that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) characterized by the function of "I-ness" (ahaṃvṛtti) is the ego (ahaṅkāra).
The second definition is its being the material cause (upādāna) of the eleven organs.
The third definition is its being the material cause of the subtle elements (tanmātra).
And its synonyms are as follows:

it is known as the ego (ahaṅkāra), self-conceit (abhimāna), the agent (kartṛ), and the thinker (mantṛ); it is also called the self (ātman), the individual soul (jīva), and the vital breath (prāṇa), from which all activities proceed. Thus [it is said].
And it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa that "the unqualified [elements] were proclaimed by Kūrma.
Furthermore, that ego (ahaṅkāra) is of three kinds;
as it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
This threefold ego— namely the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi characterized by Tamas— arose indeed from the Mahat.
The ten sense organs are taijasa, while the deities are vaikārika;
the eleventh here, the mind, is of both natures by virtue of its own quality.
"The creation of the elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras), however, arose from Bhūtādi; thus was the progeny produced.
The *vaikārika* is *sāttvika*, and the *taijasa* is *rājasa*.

By its own quality—in the form of assistance—it brings about excellence among all the sense organs; the meaning is that it is "of both natures," meaning it consists of both the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
And the deities of the sense organs are eleven: the Directions, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, Aśvi, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, Kāma, and Candra.
This concludes the exposition on the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Now, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are described.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, when devoid of specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*), as well as the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*) which possess them, are the subtle elements.
The general definition is: a substance possessing the qualities of sound and so forth without specific differentiation is a subtle element.
The second definition is: being the originator of a distinct principle while having egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) as its material cause.
The definition of each respective subtle element (*tanmātra*) is the possession of its own specific quality.
These five are: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
The specific qualities—tranquil, terrible, and deluded—are indeed particular universals (jāti-viśeṣa) pervaded by [the general universals] such as sound-ness (śabdatva) and touch-ness (sparśatva).

In the case of sound, however, there are the accents: acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (svarita); and the musical notes: niṣāda, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, ṣaḍja, madhyama, dhaivata, and pañcama.
In the case of touch, there are coldness and heat.
In the case of form (*rūpa*), the specific qualities are whiteness and so forth;
these consist of white, yellow, red, dark, green, and brown.
In the case of taste (*rasa*), the specific qualities are sweetness and so forth; these are the six tastes: sweet, bitter, astringent, pungent, sour, and salty.
Regarding smell, there are the states of being fragrant and non-fragrant;

those devoid of these specific qualities (viśeṣa) are the "non-specific" (aviśeṣa). Substances possessing these [non-specific qualities] are the "merely-that" (tanmātra). Their synonyms are: tanmātras, tamovigrahas, sūkṣmavigrahas, sūkṣmabhūtas, and aviśeṣas.
Thus are the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
Thus, the eight primary natures have been explained.
[The sixteen transformations // Tats_2 //] "The sixteen transformations" is the second aphorism.
The eleven sense organs and the five gross elements— these are the sixteen transformations.

Among these, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) because they produce cognitions of their respective objects. The voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the five organs of action (*karmendriya*) because they perform their respective functions. Among these, the function of the voice is articulation; that of the hands is grasping; that of the feet is locomotion; that of the anus is excretion; and that of the genitals is pleasure.
Because it assists all [the senses], the mind (manas) is of a dual nature.
These are the eleven sense-faculties (indriya). One definition is: being the material cause (upādāna) of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) while not producing any other fundamental principles (tattva).
The second [definition] is: that which is conjoined with the body, is an instrument of action, and is supersensuous, while being derived from the appropriation of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Now, the synonyms are: indriyas, karaṇas, nipātanas, vaikārikas, and taijasas.
Thus ends the definition of the sense organs.
Now, the great elements (mahābhūta) are earth, water, fire, air, and space.
One definition of being a great element is the possession of sound and so forth, along with their specific qualities.
The second definition is the state of being a producer while not producing other categories of reality (*tattvāntara*).

Possessing the quality of sound with its specific distinctions is the definition of space (*ākāśa*). Possessing both sound and touch with their specific distinctions is the definition of air (*vāyu*).
Fire possesses specific sound, touch, and form;
water possesses specific sound, touch, form, and taste;
and earth possesses specific sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
These are the specific characteristics.
These five great elements (mahābhūta) are mutually supportive.
Now, here are their synonyms.

The elements, the modifications, the particulars, the forms, those whose nature is darkness—whether peaceful, terrible, or deluded—thus the sixteen modifications have been explained. [The Puruṣa. (Tats 3)
"Puruṣa" is the third aphorism.

Its essential nature consists of being beginningless, subtle, conscious, all-pervading, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), immutable (kūṭastha), eternal, the witness, the enjoyer, the knower of the field (kṣetravit), mindless, and not subject to procreation. "Immutable and eternal" constitutes a single defining characteristic.
The state of being the primary enjoyer is another definition;
the state of being the witness of the mental modifications is the third definition.
Now, the synonyms are: Puruṣa, Ātman, Pum, Pudgala, Jantu, Jīva, Kṣetrajña, Nara, Kavi, Brahma, Akṣara, Prāṇa, Jña, Yaḥ, Kaḥ, and Saḥ—these are the one.
Thus, these are the twenty-five principles; by knowing them, one has accomplished all that is to be done.
And so it was said by Pañcaśikha in an authoritative statement:
"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he dwells in,"
Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.

And that person (puruṣa) is manifold, according to the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra*: "The plurality of persons is established from the distinction between pleasure, pain, and delusion, and from the distinction between birth, death, bondage, and liberation.
If there were only one person, then when one is happy, all would be happy; this being the case everywhere, the plurality of persons is thus established.

Thus, the Sāṃkhya teachers—Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, Patañjali, and others—as well as the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, [assert] many persons as the self (*ātman*), based on the principle that "there is nothing whatsoever beyond this."
The teachers of the Upaniṣads—such as Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vyāsa, and others—declare that there is one single, eternal Lord who transcends these [individual souls] and is the self of all.
Why is this so? Because it is said: "The Person alone is all this."
"That indeed is Agni, that is Āditya;

that is the Imperishable, that is the all-pervading, the most excellent, than which there is nothing higher or lower. For He alone is the Great Self dwelling in all beings, both the stationary and the moving, by whom all this is pervaded."
The wise perceive the same form in a Brahmin, in worms and insects, in an outcaste, in a cow, in an elephant, and in beasts, gadflies, and mosquitoes.
Just as a single thread passes through gold,
and likewise through pearls, gems, coral, clay, and silver;
In the same way among cattle and humans, and likewise among elephants, deer, and so forth,
this single Self is to be known as established everywhere.
This is according to such authorities as these.
The Sāṃkhyas, however, interpret these scriptural statements as referring either to the Primordial Puruṣa or to pure consciousness devoid of attributes that remains after dissolution.
Thus ends the exposition of the Puruṣa.
Thus the twenty-five principles have been explained, as well as the Sāṃkhyakārikā:
"Root nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved."
"The sixteenfold is the transformation; the Puruṣa is neither nature (prakṛti) nor transformation.

Now, although nature consisting of the qualities (guṇas) has already been indicated by the very first aphorism, this present aphorism proceeds in order to distinguish the intermediate divisions of those qualities and their attributes, and as an introductory prelude to the forthcoming discussion on the processes of cosmic evolution and dissolution.
[The Nature of the Three Attributes // TS 4 //] "The nature of the three attributes" is the fourth aphorism.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three attributes (guṇas). Their aggregate is the triad of attributes (triguṇa); the state of being that very triad of attributes is "the nature of the three attributes" (traiguṇya).
In this context, *sattva* is characterized by luminosity, lightness, clarity, attachment, joy, patience, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is pleasure.
*Rajas* is characterized by grief, distress, perspiration, paralysis, agitation, madness, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is pain.
*Tamas* is characterized by non-giving, lack of merit, wretchedness, heaviness, laziness, sleep, negligence, and so forth; it has infinite subdivisions, but in brief, its nature is delusion.
Their characteristics are as follows:
one should know that *sattva* is illuminating, *rajas* is impelling, and *tamas* is characterized by dissolution; this is what is designated as the "three qualities" (*traiguṇya*).
All these three qualities are the causes of origination, persistence, and dissolution.

Thus, the three qualities (traiguṇya) have been explained. Now, two aphorisms are set forth to demonstrate the creation and dissolution, in order to establish the validity of the scriptural passages concerning the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa), and to show the Self-born (svayambhū) produced at the beginning of creation, as well as the undifferentiated universal consciousness (citsāmānya) that remains at the time of dissolution.
[Evolution // Tats_5 //] [Dissolution // Tats_6 //] Evolution and dissolution.
Evolution is creation and re-evolution is dissolution.
Among these, creation is as follows:
primordial nature (prakṛti), known as the unmanifest, has the inherent nature of activity and is independent.

At the beginning of creation, having become agitated by herself and serving as the seed for the future Nārāyaṇa, she unites with the manifest Nārāyaṇa-puruṣa named Svayambhūpālaka from the previous kalpa; thereafter, merging with other portions of Prakṛti that are of the same nature but varying in degree, she initiates the Mahat-tattva, which consists of both sentient and insentient matter.

If it is objected that if the Puruṣa is conjoined with Prakṛti, it contradicts the scriptural statement, "This Puruṣa is indeed unattached," we say no; for the word "attachment" (saṅga) refers specifically to a conjunction that causes modification. Otherwise, the scriptural and traditional texts would not employ the lotus leaf in contact with water as an illustration of non-attachment.

In that regard, for the *mahattattva*, there is primary origination by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), whereas for the conscious principle (*cetana*), its state as an effect consists in manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
According to the words cited by Vyāsa in the *Yogabhāṣya*, there are nine kinds of being an effect:
origination, subsistence, manifestation, modification, cognition, attainment, [decrease, increase, and destruction]. (YBh 4.3)
"Separation, otherness, and maintenance are remembered as the ninefold cause.

Thus, this primordial power (*ādi-śakti*), which is a specific form of consciousness, arises spontaneously in the *svayambhū* (self-existent) waters and so forth due to its connection with the three *guṇas* that constitute the cause of the *mahat-tattva*.
And the proof for its arising is found in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Therefore, she has emerged eternally, all-pervading, and born from Viṣṇu.
And in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) attained oneness with the Śiva-principle."
"Then, at the beginning of creation, it vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed. Thus it is said in the *Pañcarātra* as well:
"Having thus beheld that Śakti, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss..."
She whose nature is the foundational empowerment for the manifestation of the abode of all the principles (tattvas).
"The Supreme Person makes that eternal Prakṛti manifest.
Thus [it is said]. The Mother of the World, Sarasvatī, the Mother of the Vedas, the Power consisting of the three qualities, appeared; she is known as Mūlaprakṛti (the Root-Nature).
From the words of Śiva, "I was born from her through those principles beginning with Mahat," and so forth,

she alone is the presiding deity of Prakṛti, designated in the Purāṇas and other texts by such terms as Mahālakṣmī, Ambā, Bhavānī, Haimavatī, and Durgā. And she, having united with the Primordial Person (Ādipuruṣa) through her playful incarnations (līlāvigrahas), protects the creation.
This has been stated by Śaṅkarācārya:
"If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is able to manifest; if it were not so, the Lord would indeed not be capable of even a movement."
In this way, the simultaneous arising of all principles (tattvas) and their respective deities is to be understood;
however, the sequence of arising follows the order of their description.

From this great [principle], which is infused with various qualities, the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) arises—consisting of both sentient and insentient aspects—namely, the *vaikārika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa*.

Then, from the ego (ahaṅkāra), preceded by volition (saṅkalpa), the body, the sense organs, and the five subtle elements (tanmātra) arise. From the *vaikārika* [ego] come the sense organs in the form of deities, and from the *taijasa* [ego] come the individual sense organs. Among those sense organs, the mind (manas) arises first.
For one whose self is purified, the ear is born from an attachment to sound.
Likewise, from attachment to form, the eye [arises]; and the nose, from the desire to smell odors.
Because it is heard in the *Mokṣadharma* and other texts that the ear and the other senses have as their effects mental functions such as attachment (*rāga*),
and because there is no relationship of cause and effect between the sense organs and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there is no fixed order [of creation].
In that regard, there is no intermediate causal relationship among the sense organs themselves, due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*).

However, that [subtle element] exists within the *tanmātras*. For instance, from the *ahaṃkāra* arises the *śabda-tanmātra*; from that *śabda-tanmātra*, which has arisen from the *ahaṃkāra* and is accompanied by the *ahaṃkāra*, arises the *sparśa-tanmātra*, which possesses the dual qualities of sound and touch.
In this manner, through the successive increase of one quality at each step, the triad of *tanmātras* is produced.
And from those *tanmātras*, the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) are born.

Regarding that, the sequence for the production of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) from ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and through them the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*), is stated in the Purāṇa as follows:
"The *bhūtādi* (the ego in its aspect as the source of elements), undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of sound alone;
from that arose space, which is hollow and characterized by sound."
Space, undergoing transformation, indeed produced the mere quality of touch;
from that, wind arises, and touch is considered its specific attribute.
"In this sequence," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since even the four elements beginning with space would become a *prakṛti* (material cause) of another principle, the established doctrine—that there are only eight *prakṛtis* and no mere *vikṛtis* (evolutes)—would be undermined.

This is not so, because the Purāṇas state that space and the other elements possess causality toward the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) such as touch only by means of the support (*upaṣṭambha*) provided by the *ahaṃkāra*.
Thus is the creation of the twenty-three principles (*tattva*).

Among these, excluding the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) and including the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) within the intellect (*buddhi*), there arises that which is known as the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), consisting of seventeen components;
for it is the locus of the manifestation of the Self (*ātman*), just as fuel is for fire.

And that [subtle body] arises for all persons at the beginning of creation through its conjunction with *prakṛti*, which serves as their respective seed, and it persists until the dissolution of *prakṛti*.
By means of that very [subtle body], the transmigratory wandering (*saṃsaraṇa*) of living beings occurs between this world and the next.

Furthermore, since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is merely a specific modification (*vṛttibheda*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not mentioned separately in the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), as it is included within the intellect itself.

And the support of that subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) consists of the five extremely subtle great elements (*mahābhūta*), with fire (*tejas*) as the predominant factor; for, like a painting, it is impossible to travel to another world without a support.
As it is said in the *Saptati*:
"Just as a painting cannot exist without a support, or as a shadow cannot exist without a post or the like..."

"Likewise, the subtle body (*liṅga*) does not remain without specificities (*viśeṣa*), being without support. Thus, at the beginning, this subtle body of the *svayambhū*, the collective consciousness, arises as a single entity in the form of a totality (*samaṣṭi*) serving as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
thereafter, the individual subtle bodies (*vyaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*) of the individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*) arise from it as its constituent parts. From that...
They are differentiated from the father’s subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) like the subtle body of a son;
this has been stated in the Sāṃkhyapravacana-sūtra:
"The distinction between individuals arises from the particularity of karma."
Manu has also said:
"Having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [elements] of immeasurable power with portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings."
Regarding the phrase "of the six": the "six faculties" (ṣaḍindriya) is an indicator for the entire subtle body (liṅgaśarīra).
Thus, the meaning is as follows:

the Self-existent One (svayambhū), having joined his own subtle and minute limbs of the subtle body to the portions of the self (ātmamātrā)—which are his own constituent consciousnesses—created all living beings.
Thus concludes the description of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Now follows the origin of the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*):
within the *mahat-tattva*, which is tenfold [in size], resides the *ahaṃkāra*; within that, which is likewise tenfold, resides space (*vyoma*); and within space as well...
From wind, fire arises; from fire, which possesses tenfold qualities, water likewise arises; and from within that water, which also possesses tenfold qualities, the earth is produced.
That very earth transforms into the form of an egg, which is the seed of the gross body.
Within that egg—the covering of the earth consisting of tenfold qualities—there arises, solely through the volition of Svayambhū, his gross body composed of the fourteen worlds.
With that very body, the Self-existent One is called Nārāyaṇa.
Regarding the Self-existent One, Manu also said:
"Desiring to emit various creatures from his own body, he meditated."
In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he cast the seed.
Then that golden egg came into being, radiant with a brilliance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa. He is the original creator of all beings; as Brahmā, he came into existence at the beginning.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

By the phrase "and so forth," it is meant that because the individual persons (vyaṣṭipuruṣas) emerge from that very First Person and are ultimately dissolved back into Him, He alone is designated as the one Self in both Śruti and Smṛti.

Consequently, that Nārāyaṇa, possessing the body of Virāj, having created the intermediate four-faced Brahmā upon Sumeru— which stands in the place of the pericarp of the lotus whose navel is the earth— creates others through him.
He created individual embodied beings down to the level of stationary objects;
and thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"Together with those effects and instruments produced from that body..."
"Kṣetrajñas were born from the limbs of that wise one.
As for the fact that the manifestation of the four-faced Brahmā from the navel-lotus, ears, eyes, and so forth of Nārāyaṇa reclining on Śeṣa is heard in scripture,
that should indeed be understood as occurring only during the daily creations according to the distinction of different Kalpas.

Indeed, it is only during the daily dissolutions (*dainandinapralaya*) that the manifestation of the gods—beginning with the four-faced Brahmā—occurs from the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, after they have entered and become unified within the body of Nārāyaṇa; this does not apply to the original creations (*ādisarga*), because during those daily dissolutions alone does Nārāyaṇa rest in his *līlā* form.
In this creation, the first emanation of the principle of Mahat (*mahattattva*) is preceded by intelligence and consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

Immediately after that, from the Self-born (Svayambhū) who is conditioned by those [limbs], there occurs a creation preceded by intelligence. Because they possess knowledge independent of a gross body, the deities of the limbs of the Self-born, as well as the Self-born himself, are called "bodiless gods" (videha-devas). Among them, the Self-born alone is the Lord (Īśvara), since the existence of an eternal Lord is not accepted.
The categories of deities and Īśvaras exist because their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not veiled by ignorance;
whereas the categories of individual souls (*jīva*) have limiting adjuncts that are veiled by ignorance.
It is precisely this state of having adjuncts that are either veiled or unveiled by ignorance that constitutes the distinction between the *jīva* and the *Īśvara*.
As it has been said: "He is the Lord under whose control Māyā stands; he is the individual soul (jīva) who is afflicted by her.
Thus, the transmigratory journey has been described.
In that regard, whatever is born from something else exists only through being filled out by its opposite.
Its dissolution also occurs in that very same place, precisely by way of its departure from it.
And so it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Whatever reality is born from something, that dissolves back into that very thing."
"They dissolve in reverse order and are born in successive order.
These transformations, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, are shown as gross ones for the sake of discriminating the immutable Puruṣa;
however, their subtle transformations are also recorded in the Smṛti.
"Just as the parts that are constantly being burned both exist and do not exist,
yet because they are subtle and their speed is imperceptible, they are not seen by time."
For this very reason, every insentient object is said to be eternally non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Consequently, those who fear suffering should become detached from that category of insentient things and perceive the Self alone as the ultimately real;
and ultimate reality is characterized by immutability and permanence.

In this regard, [the Self] must be distinguished from primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest by means of its superior, unique attributes, such as immutability, eternity, non-composite nature, being for its own sake, and pure consciousness alone. Now, the meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "Existence alone" (sadeva) is established: at the end of the re-absorption of the universe, that which remains is the undifferentiated universal consciousness.
That very reality is what is denoted by terms such as "Being" (sat) and "Brahman" in scriptural passages beginning with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
Its state of being "without a second," however, is due to its non-difference from Brahman, characterized by the absence of dissimilarity and non-separation.

Now, since scripture declares that remembrance of the Lord at the time of death is the cause for attaining the supreme goal, and since such remembrance is produced by contemplating the Lord as the inner self (adhyātma), as the physical elements (sādhibhūta), and as the divine powers (sādhidaiva), the division into adhyātma and so forth is established.
This is demonstrated by three verses,
among which the authoritative proof is as follows:
"And at the time of death, remembering Me alone, having cast off the body..."
"He who departs goes to my own state; there is no doubt about this.
And: "Those who know me as the Adhibhūta, the Adhidaiva, and the Adhiyajña—even at the time of death—they, with concentrated minds, know me."
[The internal (adhyātma) // Tats_7 //] [The elemental (adhibhūta) // Tats_8 //] [The divine (adhidaiva) // Tats_9 //]
The explanation of these three sūtras follows their respective order:
the intellect is the internal;
that which is to be known is the elemental.
Brahmā is the presiding deity there;
egoity is the internal self;
that which is to be conceived is the elemental sphere.
Rudra is the presiding deity there;
the mind is the internal self; that which is to be intended is the elemental sphere.
The moon is the presiding deity there;
the ear is the internal self;
that which is to be heard is the elemental sphere.
The directions are the presiding deity there;
the skin is the internal self;
and the object of touch is the elemental sphere.
Air is the presiding deity there;
the eye is the internal self;
that which is to be seen is the elemental sphere.
The sun is the presiding deity there;
the tongue is the internal self;
and taste is the elemental correlate.
Varuṇa is the deity above;
the sense of smell is the self within;
and odor is the element above.
The Earth is the presiding deity there;
Speech is the internal self;
and Utterance is the elemental substrate.
Fire is the presiding deity there;
the hand is the internal self;
that which is to be taken up is the elemental sphere.
Indra is the presiding deity there;
the feet are the internal self; that which is to be traversed is the objective world.
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there;
the anus is the internal self;
that which is to be discharged is the elemental sphere.
Mitra is the presiding deity there;
the generative organ is the internal self;
that which is to be gladdened is the elemental sphere.
Prajāpati is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) therein; thus, this triad is thirteenfold.

Among these, that which functions with reference to the self as a composite aggregate is the "internal" (adhyātma), namely the group of thirteen instruments. That which functions with reference to the elements is the "pertaining to the elements" (adhibhūta), namely the group of objects.

That which exists with reference to the deities is *adhidaivata*, meaning the group of deities presiding over the instruments [of perception]. For one who meditates upon the Lord together with these, the fruit is the supreme goal attained through the recollection of the Blessed One at the time of death.
Therefore, the sense is that this triad must necessarily be known.
Furthermore, the fruit of knowing all the principles (*tattvas*) has been stated in a passage cited by Pañcaśikha:

He who knows the principles as they truly are—their essential natures as the gunas and their presiding deities—is freed from evil and the multitude of defects; he enjoys the gunas, but he is not enjoyed by the gunas.
"Tattvas" is a technical term used in the Tantras.

Its meaning consists of those categories which serve as the counter-correlates and correlates for the discernment of the Self from the non-Self; their "state" (bhāva) refers to the grounds for the application of their respective terms, namely the twenty-five universals such as "personhood" (puruṣatva), "primordial nature" (prakṛtitva), and so forth. Due to the non-difference between attribute and substrate, the individual manifestations are also called "tattvas."
"Experiences" (vedayate) means "knows" (vetti).

The qualities (guṇāḥ) are sattva, rajas, and tamas; those whose very natures (svarūpa) or essential forms (tāttvika-rūpa) are these [qualities] are "those whose nature consists of the qualities" (guṇasvarūpāṇi). "And with respect to the deities" (adhidaivatam) is an elliptical expression for "with respect to the deities, the self, and the elements" (adhyātmādhibhūta).
[The meaning is: he experiences the qualities, and the qualities remain under his control.
He is not consumed by the qualities; the meaning is that he does not come under the sway of the qualities.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Tattvapāda.

Now the second miscellaneous section (prakīrṇakapāda) begins. Therein, for the sake of establishing the meaning of such scriptural passages as "We meditate upon [the river] which has five currents of water, five fierce wheels of birth, five waves of vital breaths, five roots beginning with the intellect, five whirlpools, the forceful current of the flood of the five sufferings, fifty divisions, and five joints," there are the pentads (pañcakas).
He defines it by means of a collection of sūtras.
[The five types of resolve (abhibuddhi):
Resolve, conceit, desire, the sense of duty, and action—these are the five associated with resolve.
Among these, "resolve" (abhibuddhi) means an intellect directed toward an object; it is a mental modification in the form of the thought, "This must certainly be done."
Abhimāna is the mental state [of ego] thinking "I am doing this. Icchā (desire) and vāñchā (longing) are mental states of volition.
Kartavyatā is the functioning of the organs of cognition toward objects such as sound and so forth.
Action, characterized by speech and so forth, is the function of the organs of action.
The higher cognitions have been explained.
[The five wombs of action (pañca karmayonayaḥ):
Those born of action and those generating action are fivefold: steadfastness, faith, happiness, the desire to know, and the desire to know.
He who protects his foundation in speech, action, and resolve—being established in that and resting upon that—is characterized by fortitude; for this indeed is the mark of dhṛti.
Freedom from envy, celibacy, performing sacrifices,
officiating at sacrifices, austerity, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and offering oblations are recorded as the characteristics of faith.
But for one who seeks wealth and serves through learning, ritual action, and austerity,
and is constantly devoted to expiation— this is proclaimed as the easy path.
*Avividiṣā* is the activity that obstructs the desire to know the Vedas.
As for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*):
unity and diversity, that which is eternal, insentient, subtle, the existent effect, and unshakeable— that indeed is to be known as the desire to know.
The desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is the inquiry concerning the oneness, separateness, and so forth, regarding the self.

Among these [five desires], four lead to bondage, while the desire to know leads to liberation, because it is produced by, and gives rise to, the karma that destroys the obstacles to knowledge and liberation.
[The five winds // Tats_12 //] Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna in the anus, vyāna pervades the entire body,
udāna is in the region of the throat, and samāna is situated in the navel.

These five, although they are specific modifications of the internal organ endowed with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), are called "winds" (*vāyu*) because their movement is similar to that of air and because their presiding deity is Vāyu. They are called *prāṇa* because of moving forward (*pra-anana*) or going forth; *apāna* because of moving downward (*adho-gamana*).
It is called *vyāna* because it distributes the essence and other components of the food that has been eaten, and because it causes yawning.
It is celebrated as *udāna* because it performs functions such as belching and vomiting. It is *samāna* because it leads the evenly distributed essence of the food throughout the body.
Other [winds] mentioned in other tantras—namely those called Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—are also to be included within that very [category].
Thus, these five vital breaths have been explained.
[The five agents of action (karmātmānaḥ):
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, the Bhūtādi, the Sānumāna, and the Niranumāna—these are the agents of action; the meaning is that they are performers of action (karmiṇaḥ).
Among them, the Vaikārika is the performer of auspicious actions.
The Taijasa is the performer of inauspicious actions;
the Bhūtādi is the performer of deluded actions;
and the Sānumāna is the performer of auspicious and deluded actions.
One who performs impure and deluded actions is devoid of inference.
Thus, the five whose nature is action have been explained.
Now, in order to establish the meaning of the scripture that "we study the five-knot ignorance with its fifty divisions," he indicates the fifty creations of the intellect through many aphorisms:
"[Ignorance has five knots].

Ignorance (*avidyā*), as defined by Patañjali, is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self; this is accepted by all philosophical systems.

And that [ignorance] is fivefold: ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*). They are designated as "afflictions" (*kleśa*) in the *Yoga* [system] because they generate affliction. Furthermore, since the four beginning with egoism are effects of ignorance, they are of the nature of ignorance. Egoism is the notion of "I" with respect to what is not the self. This is the distinction between ignorance and egoism: in ignorance, the locus also appears separately; in egoism, however, although it is of the nature of a superimposition, the locus does not appear.
Attachment (*rāga*) is an intense desire for sense objects;
aversion (*dveṣa*) is the thought of enmity;
and clinging (*abhiniveśa*) is the fear of death.

Even for the wise, there flows spontaneously a tendency born from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the experience of the suffering of death since time immemorial. These varieties of ignorance (*avidyā*) are designated in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas* by terms such as "darkness" (*tamas*) and so forth.
They are given those specific names because they lead to hells named after them: namely, *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*.
Furthermore, due to the diversity of their objects, they comprise sixty-two varieties, which are as follows: [The list of sixty-two varieties follows.]
Due to the superimposition of selfhood upon the eight constituent natures (*prakṛti*), darkness (*tamas*) is eightfold.
Having attained the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*, the gods harbor the conceit, "We are immortal"; this eightfold conceit is delusion (*moha*).

When the twelve objects—both those perceived by sight and those heard through tradition—are obtained, one thinks, "I am liberated"; because this conceit is caused by an excess of passion (*rāga*), it is the tenfold great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
The suffering that arises from anger in one who is obstructed in the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* and in the tenfold objects of sense is *tāmisra*; it is eighteenfold.

The gods, while enjoying the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā* and the ten objects such as sound, remain here out of fear of their [merit] being exhausted; for them, this very [suffering] is *andhatāmisra*. Thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) has sixty-two divisions and five stages.
[The powerlessness is of twenty-eight kinds.
// Tats_15 //] [Contentment is of nine kinds.
// Tats_16 //] [Success is of eight kinds. // Tats_17 //]
In that regard, the incapacities consist of the eleven impairments of the sense faculties and seventeen impairments of the intellect.
Among these, the impairments of the sense faculties consist in the incapacity for their respective functional activities; in effect, they are [impairments] of the intellect alone.
Deafness, leprosy, blindness, numbness, as well as loss of smell, muteness, lameness, crippledness, impotence, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and stupidity.
There are seventeen obstructions to the intellect (*buddhi*) itself, which are the opposites of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*).
Among these, the opposites of contentment are as follows:
the cognition that "the primal matter (*pradhāna*) does not exist" is designated as [the first obstruction].
The knowledge that the principle of Mahat does not exist is ignorance;
the notion that the ego (ahaṅkāra) does not exist is delusion;
and the view that the five subtle elements (tanmātras) do not exist at all is non-vision.
The engagement in the acquisition of sense objects is difficult to cross; the engagement in their protection is difficult to reach the further shore;
and for one who does not perceive the fault of their decay, such engagement is difficult to lead across.
The power regarding enjoyments is merely vital breath;
the engagement in enjoyment by one who does not perceive the fault of violence is "anuttamāmbhasikī.
Thus, the opposites of contentment are ninefold.
Due to the reversal of attainment, eight obstructions to intelligence are taught.
For one who conceives of multiplicity while pursuing unity, it is called "easy crossing" (*sutāra*). Grasping things erroneously by merely hearing the words is "not easy crossing" (*asutārā*).

For example, having heard that one who does not know the various selves is liberated, one may arrive at a misconception, thinking, "I am one who does not know the various selves, yet I am not unliberated.

Even for one devoted to study and hearing [the teachings], if—due to dullness or because the intellect has been impaired by false treatises—the realization of the knowledge of the twenty-five principles does not occur, that is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
When one is overwhelmed by internal suffering, that is the negligence of ignorance (*ajñānapramāda*).
Thus, one is overwhelmed by the suffering caused by other beings while rejoicing in it;
likewise, there is an overwhelming of the mind by the suffering caused by divine forces (ādhidevika) despite being joyful.
Even when instructed by a friend, a state of indecisive intellect regarding the self is useless.
Knowing one's own gift to be fruitless, yet feeling joy when great suffering has arisen for the recipient of the gift—this is *pramuditā*.
Thus, the eight reversals of success (*siddhi*) have been explained.
In this way, there are seventeen obstructions to intelligence (*buddhivadha*).
Ninefold contentment is thus described; regarding this, there is a verse:
"The four internal [contentments] are named nature, acquisition, time, and fortune."
The five external and nine [internal] contentments have been described as resulting from the cessation of attachment to sense objects.

The contentment that arises from hearing, "Nature itself, transforming in some way through all its modes, will produce knowledge," is called *prakṛti*; thus, it has the designation of being [the first].

The contentment that arises from undertaking renunciation upon hearing, "Knowledge will come about through renunciation alone," is designated as *salila*. The contentment that arises after a long period of time following renunciation upon hearing, "Knowledge will come about through time alone," is called *ādyā* (the first).
The contentment that arises from hearing from someone that "knowledge will come by destiny alone, just as it does for children," is called *vṛṣṭi*.
These four are internal (*ādhyātmika*).

Now, regarding the five external ones: among those satisfactions of withdrawal resulting from perceiving the defects in the objects of the senses—such as sound—namely acquisition, preservation, decay, enjoyment, and injury, one [is described].

Contentment is said to be "without the far shore" (apāra), the second is "well-crossed" (supāra), the third is "the far shore" (pāra), the fourth is "in the unsurpassed water" (anuttamāmbhasikā), and the fifth is "the supreme water" (uttamāmbhas); thus the nine contentments have been explained.
Now, there are eight perfections (*siddhi*). Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Inference, verbal testimony, study, the three types of removal of suffering, and the acquisition of friends."
There is generosity and the eight accomplishments; prior to accomplishment is the threefold hook.
The meaning of this is as follows:
through the power of the Blessed One’s compassion, knowledge arises by means of inference and reasoning alone; that is the first accomplishment, called *Tārā*.
That knowledge which arises from the mere hearing of the sound [of the teaching] is the second, *Sutārā*.
The knowledge [attained] through study in the capacity of a disciple is the third, *tāratārā*.
The knowledge that dispels internal suffering is the fourth, *pramodā*. The knowledge that dispels suffering caused by external beings is the fifth, *pramuditā*.

The sixth stage, *pramodamānā*, is that knowledge which destroys suffering caused by divine or supernatural forces; the seventh, *ramyakā*, is that knowledge [attained] through association with virtuous friends;
and the eighth, *sadāmuditā*, is that knowledge [received] from a teacher who has been fully satisfied by one's gifts.

Among these, the first three are the "restraining hook"—meaning the attractor or achiever—of the three primary accomplishments (*siddhi*) whose nature is the destruction of suffering; indeed, these alone are the true accomplishments.
As for *aṇimā* and the others, they are actually non-accomplishments (*asiddhi*) because they act as obstacles to knowledge; such is the intention of the Teacher.
Thus, the eight accomplishments have been explained.

Now, in order to establish that the Sāṃkhya treatise consists of sixty topics (*ṣaṣṭitantra*), he completes the other ten among the fifty chapters on the attainment of perfections (*siddhisarga*) with this aphorism:
"There are ten root-meanings: existence, unity, lack of correspondence to reality, being for the sake of another, difference, and non-agency. (Tats_18)
Union, separation, the plurality of souls, the persistence of the body, and the remaining mode of subsistence.
The "root-meanings" (*mūlikārtha*) are the properties (*dharma*) of the two roots, namely *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
Among these, existence (*astitva*) is a property common to both; oneness (*ekatva*) belongs to *prakṛti*, consisting in the absence of plurality despite the diversity of creation;
and purposefulness (*arthavattva*), meaning being for the sake of the *puruṣa*, belongs to the *puruṣa* alone.
The state of being for the sake of another belongs to primordial nature alone;
distinctness from the category of the insentient belongs to the person alone;
and the state of being a non-agent belongs to the person alone.
Union and disunion belong to both [the *puruṣa* and the *prakṛti*];
multiplicity belongs to the *puruṣa* alone.

That persistence of the body of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), which occurs through the mere force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) like the whirling of a potter's wheel, is the "remaining function" (*śeṣavṛtti*) of the *puruṣa*.
Thus, there are ten categories known as the "evolution of cognition" (*pratyayasarga*), which together with the fifty previously mentioned constitute these ten root categories;
in this way, sixty categories are taught in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*.
Now he formulates the sūtra concerning the creation of the five subtle elements (pañcatanmātra):
[The creation of favor (anugrahasarga) // TS 19 //] That creation which occurs by favoring— that is, by accepting as material causes— the five subtle elements, is the creation of favor.

The creation of the five Brahmins—namely Caturmukha, Sanaka, and the others—within his own *līlā-vigraha* for the sake of favoring his devotees is also an *anugraha-sarga*, and it proceeds from the five *tanmātras* alone.
Now he describes the creation of beings:
[The creation of beings is of fourteen kinds.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 20)] The eight divine creations are those of the Brahmas, the Prājāpatis, the Saumyas, the Indras, the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, and the Piśācas.
The animal kingdom consists of five types: domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and stationary beings.
Human beings constitute one type, ranging from Brahmins down to Caṇḍālas. Domestic animals range from cows down to mice.
Birds range from the *garuḍa* down to the gnat;
wild animals range from the lion down to the jackal; and reptiles range from the serpent *śeṣa* down to the *dundubha*.
"From mountains down to grass, these are the stationary beings.
Here is a verse:
"The divine [realm] is of eight kinds; the animal realm..."
"And it [the elemental creation] is fivefold;
and the human is of one kind—thus, in brief, is the elemental creation.
This circle of saṃsāra indicates other creations not yet mentioned by means of three sūtras.
[Binding is threefold. // Tattvasaṃgraha 21 //] [Liberation is threefold. // Tattvasaṃgraha 22 //] [The means of valid cognition is threefold. // Tattvasaṃgraha 23 //]
There are three types of bondage: the natural (*prākṛtika*), the modified (*vaikṛtika*), and the external (*dākṣiṇa*).
The natural consists of the form of ego-identification with the eight constituent principles (*prakṛtis*).
The second, however, is the attachment of the mind to sound and other sense objects even among those who have renounced the world.
The third, however, is the "bondage of sacrificial fees" (dakṣiṇā-bandha) for householders and others whose minds are afflicted by desire as they bestow sacrificial fees.
And it has been said by the teacher Pañcaśikha:
"Bound by the natural (prākṛta) bond, as well as by the modified (vaikārika), and by the third, that of ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), the living being transmigrates. Thus,
the threefold nature of liberation has been stated.
First, liberation is through knowledge; second, through the destruction of passion;
and third, through the exhaustion of suffering. Thus has the definition of liberation been explained.

The first [type of liberation] consists in the cessation of ignorance through the intensification of knowledge; the second consists in the subsiding of the senses through the destruction of attachment; and the third consists in the non-production of merit and demerit through the exhaustion of existing merit and demerit.
These three constitute a secondary triad of liberations because they serve as gateways to knowledge.
The primary liberation is simply the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering.

This has been stated by Gautama in the Sūtra: "Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the non-existence of each preceding one, which constitutes liberation.
To establish the categories (padārtha) thus mentioned, he states the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because the establishment of the objects of cognition depends upon the means of cognition.
"The means of valid cognition is threefold."
[The means of valid cognition are] perception, inference, and verbal testimony.
Among these, the first general definition is: valid cognition (*pramā*) is a cognition that apprehends an object as it truly is, and its instrument (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of that [cognition].
The second [definition] is: [valid cognition is] an internal mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) that assumes the form of the object and apprehends it as it truly is.
In this context, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is valid perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapramā*), which is a true knowledge produced by the sense organs that has not been previously apprehended.
The instrument (*karaṇa*) for that is the means of valid perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
A second definition is: a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) produced by the sense organs, which is a true knowledge not previously apprehended.

The first definition is: inference (*anumiti*) is the knowledge arising from the knowledge of a mark (*liṅga*) that is in accordance with reality, and the instrument (*karaṇa*) of that is inference (*anumāna*).
The second is: it is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*), arising from the knowledge of the mark.

The first definition of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*) is: verbal valid cognition is the knowledge produced by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), and its instrument is the means of verbal valid cognition.

The second definition of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is: "An internal modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) of the nature of the non-connection of word-meanings, produced by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*).
A reliable person (*āpta*), however, is one who is devoted to his own duty, free from passion and hatred, possessed of knowledge, and endowed with virtuous conduct.
This, indeed, is the definition of a reliable person as a teacher of knowledge; in reality, it is simply a person who teaches a matter exactly as it is.

Among the categories of objects mentioned, some are established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and some are established through inference (*anumāna*). That which is not established by either of these two is established by the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*), such as: "Indra is the king of the gods," "the Northern Kurus," "Mount Meru is golden," and "there are celestial nymphs (*apsarasaḥ*) in heaven. These objects are not accessible through perception or inference, but are accessible solely through verbal testimony.

And here, this is the process of cognition: the "modification" (vṛtti) is accepted as the undivided, yet contracting and expanding, tip of the internal organ and the senses; for it is stated in the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra* that "the modification, being distinct from the [organ] as a part or a quality, extends itself for the sake of connection."

A "part" (*bhāga*) is a divided portion; therefore, that which is not a part—that is, an undivided portion—is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*), meaning a distinct category of existence (*padārthāntara*). Thus, the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) comes into contact with the object by means of the modification of the sense organ (*indriyavṛtti*); subsequently, together with the modification of the sense organ, it transforms into the form of the object. And that modification, which takes the form of the object and consists of the *guṇas*, [appears] only in its own respective master-self (*svasvāmī*), even though all selves are omnipresent (*vibhu*).

It is reflected nowhere else, because the relationship between water and its possessor (the moon) is the regulator of reflection; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the reflection is a modification (*vikāra*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) residing in the substrate. "Ownership" (*svattva*) consists in possessing the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a mental state (*vṛtti*) manifested by its possessor. "Possessor-ship" (*svāmitva*) consists in being the manifester of the mental state that generates the latent impression residing in itself; and that mental state resides in the Self (*ātman*).

When the existent [cognition], possessing the form of the object and the form of the self, assumes another modification (pariṇāmāntara) that has a form identical to its own, that very thing is the reflection of the mental mode (vṛtti-pratibimba) within the self; this is the relation called "objectivity" (viṣayatā). Consciousness delimited by that [relation] is perceptual valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramā), which has as its objects both the thing and the self in the form "I know the jar. Thus it has been said.
Just as the invisible Rāhu is perceived by means of the eclipsed moon,
so too is the self, whose nature is pure experience, beheld through that which is perceptible.
By means of the visible object,
this direct modification (*pratyakṣā vṛttiḥ*) arises at the location of the object and is reflected right there within the self (*ātman*), because of the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the self.

Furthermore, wherever the mind, by the power of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), becomes connected with an object without the mediation of the sense organs, there it assumes the form of that object.
The mode [of perception] is mental direct perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa).
And it has been said:
"Where the bird of the mind, having abandoned its resting place in the body, [remains]."
Under the influence of its own latent impressions, the self proceeds to that very place where it is experienced.
Thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha.
This concludes the section on direct perception.

Thus, inference (*anumāna*) is the verbal expression whose form is the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*), produced by the valid cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*); the consciousness delimited by the reflection thereof is inferential knowledge (*anumiti*).
Such is the process of inference.

The modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the recollection of words according to their actual meaning, which takes the form of the connection between word-meanings, is verbal valid cognition (*śabda-pramāṇa*); the consciousness delimited by the reflection therein is verbal valid knowledge (*śābdī pramā*). These two—the means of knowledge and its result—are entirely internal. Whether it be immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), mediacy (*parokṣatva*), memory-ness (*smṛtitva*), doubt-ness (*saṃśayatva*), error-ness (*viparyayatva*), validity (*pramātva*), or invalidity (*apramātva*), all these are merely attributes of the mental modification (*vṛtti*). Due to the influence of that reflection, they are metaphorically attributed to consciousness (*caitanya*) as well. Among these, immediacy, mediacy, and memory-ness...
Generality (*jāti*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*) are functions that touch upon both sides of a manifest contradiction.

Where something does not exist, the certain cognition thereof is error (*viparyaya*). Cognition whose function accords with reality is valid knowledge (*pramā*); cognition whose function does not accord with reality is invalid knowledge (*apramā*). Regarding this subject of the division between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, there is a verse by the Teacher Vijñāna: "The knower is the pure conscious self; the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the mental modification (*vṛtti*)."
The reflection of the functions of ultimate forms within consciousness.
The object of the reflected mental modifications (vṛtti) is called the "knowable" (meyam);
the modifications themselves are manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), as they do not depend upon any further instrument (karaṇa).
"And the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*), which consists in direct perception, is set forth in the Sāṃkhya Sūtras.

Furthermore, the fact that knowledge is produced, perishable, and an attribute of the self must be established by way of its being delimited by a reflection (*pratibimba*); for knowledge, insofar as it is of the nature of the self, is eternal.

This is according to the logical principle that "prescriptions and prohibitions apply to the qualified [subject], and when there is an obstruction regarding the qualified [subject], they transfer to the qualifier."

The relationship of container and contained is also to be understood as in the case of "the rising of birds in the sky"; this serves as the proof for the reflection of the mental modifications within the Self.

And in that expansive mirror, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as the trees on the bank are reflected in a lake: "In that vast mirror, all these perceptions of things are reflected, just as the trees on the shore are reflected in a lake."
Thus ends the Vāsiṣṭha;
thus concludes, in brief, the method of knowledge.

In this treatise, even those categories not explicitly mentioned that do not contradict its own principles are to be accepted from other systems, according to the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra*: "One should take the essence [from elsewhere], like a bee from flowers," and the *Smṛti*: "One should gather the essence from everywhere, just as a bee does from flowers.

Now, these categories such as *prakṛti* and the rest are to be abandoned because they are flawed by defects such as being composite, being objects, being insentient, and undergoing transformation at every moment; moreover, he states what is to be abandoned even more than these:
[There are three kinds of suffering:
internal, external, and celestial.
Among these, the internal is twofold: bodily and mental.
Among these, bodily suffering arises from the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), such as fever, diarrhea, and the like;

mental suffering is born of desire, anger, greed, and so forth; suffering caused by other beings (*ādhibhautika*) arises from humans, wild animals, snakes, and the like; and suffering caused by the divine or supernatural (*ādhidaivika*) arises from cold, heat, wind, and rain.
Upon hearing the Vedic scripture, "He who knows the Self overcomes sorrow," a desire to know the Self arises in one who is overwhelmed by these three kinds of suffering.

Just as one who is thirsty has a craving for water, [the author] shows the connection between the investigation of reality and the human goal: "This is the ultimate accordance with reality; having known this, one becomes one who has accomplished what was to be done and is no longer overcome by the threefold suffering. (Tattvasaṃgraha 25)

The meaning is this: "this reality" (*etadyāthārthya*) is supreme, being superior to the reality taught in other scriptures; for while the reality taught in Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika is incomplete due to its failure to mention the eight *prakṛtis*, this [teaching] is complete because it does mention them, and it is supreme—meaning most excellent—because it is in accord with the Śruti.
And the Śruti, in the Gopālatāpanīya, states: "Brahman alone was one without a second; from that Unmanifest [came] the Unmanifest, which is indeed the Imperishable (*akṣara*)."

Therefore, it is clearly heard that creation proceeds according to the sequence of Mahat and the rest as taught in Sāṃkhya and Yoga: from [Prakṛti] comes Mahat, from Mahat comes Ahaṃkāra, from that come the five Tanmātras, and from those the elements (bhūtāni).

Having known this, one becomes "one who has accomplished all that was to be done" (kṛtakṛtya) by means of the direct realization of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; the meaning is that one becomes free from further purposeful activity (niṣprayojana).
What, then, is that purpose? To this he says:
"Furthermore, one is not overcome by the threefold suffering.
The meaning is that one is no longer joined with the threefold suffering previously mentioned; liberation occurs in the form of the absolute cessation of suffering.
Now, suffering is indeed threefold: future, present, and past.
According to the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta schools, which rely on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), every effect is eternal throughout its three states.
This is because, even across the three states—the future pot, the present pot, and the past pot—there is a continuous cognition of the pot as the underlying substrate (*dharmin*) of those states.

Furthermore, since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) are not accepted [as real entities], one should not ask how the cognition of non-existence occurs at those times; for that is accounted for by means of a temporal absolute non-existence (*sāmayikātyantābhāva*) whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is present. Thus, even though there is a non-existence of future and past suffering, it does not constitute the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because only the non-existence of suffering that is to be experienced constitutes the human goal.

Furthermore, present suffering, even though it is an object of experience, will perish through experience alone; therefore, its non-existence is not the *puruṣārtha* (the goal of man), because it is independent of human effort, whereas only that which depends on human effort constitutes a *puruṣārtha*. Thus, how can the non-existence of suffering be a *puruṣārtha* both by being the cause of an object of experience and by being achievable through human action? [The answer is: It is a *puruṣārtha* because human activity is directed toward the eradication of the causes of suffering, just as in the case of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
This was stated by Patañjali in two sūtras: "That which is to be abandoned is future suffering; the means of its abandonment is the uninterrupted flow of discriminative discernment.

Furthermore, for the Sāṃkhyas, since there is no difference in nature among all selves, the meaning of the statement "That thou art" is simply non-difference, not non-distinction; for it is the knowledge of that [non-difference] alone which removes the conceit of individuality.

Furthermore, that statement was uttered precisely for the purpose of removing Śvetaketu’s conceit regarding his status as a learned Vedic scholar (*anūcāna*) and so forth; thus, the referent of the word *tat* (That) is the universal consciousness (*cit-sāmānya*) remaining after dissolution. This has been stated by our teacher, the eminent Vijñānācārya, in the first verse of his commentary: "The Vedic declarations such as 'One, without a second' serve for the liberation of this person by turning away all his conceits;

they declare the absence of difference characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-lakṣaṇa-bheda*), not indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatā*), because [indivisibility] is not contradicted even by a hundred attributes, just as [the nature of] space is not."

And likewise, through the direct realization of the difference in dissimilarity (*avaidharmya-bheda*) among all selves, which are by nature distinct from *prakṛti* and the rest, there occurs the cessation of the conceit of agency (*kartṛtva-abhimāna*) and so forth; because of that, attachment, aversion, merit, and other qualities—which are their effects—do not arise. Furthermore, since previously arisen karmas do not initiate rebirth and the like due to the destruction of their auxiliary causes such as ignorance and attachment, and because there is no further birth after the completion of commenced karma (*prārabdha*) through experience, there follows the simultaneous fulfillment of both experience and liberation (*bhoga-apavarga*).

Liberation, which consists in the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering through the very destruction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), constitutes the state of having accomplished the supreme task.

Furthermore, it should be noted here that even knowledge produced from the instructions of a teacher and the study of scriptures must indeed be practiced for the sake of attaining direct perception (*aparokṣatva*).

Because without that [direct realization], there is no possibility of removing immediate ignorance; for it is determined that in the case of an immediate error, only a certain conviction that is immediate and has the same objective referent (*viśeṣya*) as the error can remove it. As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Even by one who has realized the truth, this [negation] must always be practiced as 'not so'."
The kataka fruit does not clarify water by its name alone.
"Verbal knowledge is indeed not capable of destroying internal darkness;
O Rāma, darkness is not destroyed by the mere report of a lamp.

Thus, when knowledge has arisen through such practice—according to the maxim of the "soft thorn"—the yogi is said to be "established in yoga" (*yogarūḍha*); prior to this stage he was "practicing yoga" (*yuñjāna*). Thereafter, by means of the stage of the *paramahaṃsa*, [he abandons] those actions that cause distraction.
Having abandoned [the path of action], one should practice until reaching the culmination of knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*).
The culmination of knowledge is the eradication of ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-avidyoccheda*).
Consequently, he is called "one who is disciplined," "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*), and "one who has transcended the qualities" (*guṇātīta*).

The state of being beyond the qualities (*guṇātītatva*) is precisely the absence of pride regarding those qualities, and it is the defining characteristic of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets, and who remains as he was before in the face of pleasure and pain— he is called liberated while living.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
he who remains as pure as the inner sky is called one liberated in this very life.

"Indeed, this alone is the sign of one who has known [the Truth]—the formless one whose long wandering through the cycle of transmigration has been stilled and who is at peace: that his passion, anger, dejection, delusion, greed, and misfortunes daily diminish with skillful precision. Furthermore, in this context of the Sāṃkhya knowledge, it should be understood that devotion to the Blessed One (*bhagavad-bhakti*) is the unique cause; otherwise, the destruction of yoga certainly occurs due to obstacles created by the gods, as it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*.
O Lotus-eyed One, others who consider themselves liberated, whose intellects are impure because they have fixed their devotion on you [only partially],
ascend with great difficulty to the highest state and then fall down from it, having failed to honor your feet.

"O Lord, those who cast aside devotion to You—the hearing of which leads to the highest good—and strive for the sake of attaining mere intellectual knowledge, for them only that very effort remains as a source of weariness, and nothing else, just like those who thresh coarse husks. Thus [it is said]. Now, certain contemporary Vaiṣṇavas, placing devotion to the Blessed One at the forefront, generally disparage the path of knowledge; however, they are of dull intellect and ignorant of the discrimination of true wisdom.
And likewise, in the *Nāradīya* Purāṇa, in the section on the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, it is said:
"When firm devotion is established by men toward Viṣṇu, the initiator of Māyā..."
Through bliss, it reveals its own nature as distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti), like a lamp.
For when the mind is under one's own control, yoga succeeds; but who, without relying on the Lord of the Universe, could restrain that which is unmanifest and exceedingly fickle?
"Therefore, for one desiring liberation, the path of taking refuge in Śrī Viṣṇu is most blissful;
by thinking otherwise, one is certainly deceived.
Thus it is said in the fourteenth chapter of the Gītā.
"And he who serves Me with unswerving devotion, having transcended the *guṇas* indeed, is fit for becoming Brahman" (Gītā 14.26).

For the sake of "becoming Brahman"—that is, for manifestation in fullness—the mention of the *guṇas* is because one is manifested precisely through being delimited by them; therefore, devotion to the Blessed Lord alone is the primary means in the science of Sāṃkhya-yoga.
Success! This illumination of the true nature of reality has been composed for the benefit of others. By this, may Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self and Teacher of the World, be pleased with me.
Because of his independence, he alone—the Great Lord known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa—is the sole agent; I am like a wooden puppet.
This has been spoken by me for those who desire to know the meaning of the Purāṇas;
it is offered to them, and through this, may Hari be pleased.
Thus ends the *Tattvayāthārthyadīpana*, composed by Bhāvagaṇeśa, son of Śrī Bhāvāviśvanātha Dīkṣita.
